title: The Best Study Abroad in Italy
paragraphs: From February 2025, I did clerkships for three months at the University of Bologna and the Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna Policlinico di Sant'Orsola-Malpighi in Italy. Surrounded by a rich culture, cheerful people, historic architecture and delicious food, I had a valuable, irreplaceable experience in three months and it became a memory I will never forget. I would like to introduce my clerkship life and daily life.

The University of Bologna is a university with so much history that it is said to be the oldest university in the world. While my heart raced at being given the opportunity to do clerkships at such a university, since this was the first year of dispatches to Italy, there was little advance information and I was also very anxious. So I tried to collect as much information as possible by getting information from students of the University of Bologna who had come to Nagoya University and by searching online. Also, Bologna is a student city, and students gather from all over the world. The medical school also has an English course, in which one can study for the six years. For this reason, housing shortage is a big problem, and I had a great deal of trouble finding lodging for the short period of three months. As for language, for about half a year after my study abroad in Italy was decided I studied Italian little by little with a language app called Duolingo, but to be honest I could not secure enough time, and I was very worried about whether I could get through the clerkships without being able to speak English or Italian well and whether I could communicate with the people around me during the study abroad.

The Sant'Orsola-Malpighi University Hospital is said to be the largest hospital in Italy, and patients gather from both northern and southern Italy. The hospital grounds are large and rich in nature, with a separate building for each department, and I remember being surprised from the start by the difference from the hospitals I had imagined until then, and at the same time looking forward very much to a clerkship in an unknown land. I did clerkships for four weeks each in internal medicine, gastroenterology and pediatric cardiac surgery.

●February Internal medicine (inflammatory bowel disease ward). Among the many wards, I was assigned to the inflammatory bowel disease ward. On the first day a doctor told me "This is the center for inflammatory bowel disease in Italy," and I learned that it was a particularly specialised and important department.

・Week 1. There were no local students to go around with, and I was the only student. First, rounds begin. The doctors and patients were open, so the doctors spoke to me even though I was a foreign student, and I was easily allowed to do physical examinations. Basically conversations between patients and doctors are in Italian, but the doctors always spoke to me and taught me a great deal about the patients' conditions and treatment. A doctor said, "Not everyone may speak to you in English a lot, but please feel free to ask questions in English! I'll answer anything!", and I resolved anew to always approach with a proactive attitude in order to make the most of the valuable three months to come. It was indeed as the doctor said, and when I asked questions myself, every doctor kindly taught me. After the physical examination, the doctor also asked "What are the findings?" and gave me feedback. After rounds I examined newly admitted patients and the doctors explained cases to me. Here I was allowed to take histories of newly admitted patients (the doctor interpreted) and to apply ECG electrodes. I was also allowed to observe abdominal ultrasound. The doctor explained in English, and when I asked questions they kindly taught me anything. As an aside, the professor of this department was very friendly and often looked out for me. The professor himself sometimes brought very delicious Italian sweets to the doctors' office, and the doctors said "You eat plenty too!", so I could enjoy the sweets and was very happy. I was also invited to the evening meeting (in Italian), where a doctor taught me by writing in English on a smartphone during the meeting.

・Week 2 onward. Six medical students of the University of Bologna joined, and group clerkships began. After rounds, the doctor gave us materials on inpatients, and everyone read them and discussed them, thought about what to ask the patients, and then examined and took histories from the patients, applied ECG electrodes and measured blood pressure with a stethoscope. The doctor also sometimes explained knowledge needed in any department, such as about ECGs and heart sounds. I was also happy that when I could not understand because the doctors and patients were speaking Italian, I became able to ask my friends casually.

In this way, in the four weeks of internal medicine, I could study the pathology and treatment of inflammatory bowel disease in depth, and at the same time learn knowledge needed in all departments and how to read abdominal ultrasound. I was also able to put into practice much of what I had learned in Japan, such as whole-body history-taking and physical examination (auscultation, percussion, palpation), ECG measurement and blood pressure measurement. Locally, third-year students do clerkships in this department, and I was surprised that the period of dealing with real patients and learning the clinical setting is earlier than in Japan.

●March Gastroenterology. At Sant'Orsola, gastroenterology handles the gastroenterological diseases other than inflammatory bowel disease. In endoscopy Japan leads the world, and the Japanese guidelines for gastroenterological diseases are also used in Europe, so I felt respect for Japan.

・Week 1. Ward. As I went around with first-year resident doctors, they explained things to me each time. First I accompanied the doctor on rounds, and, as in February, I applied ECG electrodes and took physical findings. I was also allowed to do simple tasks such as adding drugs to infusions. After rounds, I was given the European guidelines on EUS and papers on fecal transplantation, and was allowed to study using them. The doctors who looked after me here were also very friendly, and many liked Japanese culture such as anime, and they welcomed me by taking me to Japanese food restaurants and Italian restaurants.

・Week 2. Endoscopy. I could observe a wide range, from examinations using gastroscopes and colonoscopes to advanced procedures such as ESD, EUS-FNA and ERCP. They explained a lot about the examinations and procedures in front of me and the patients' conditions, and answered kindly when I asked questions, so I could deepen my knowledge of endoscopy and related areas, and at the same time it was very interesting to learn first-hand the parts that differ from Japan. In particular, seeing the resection of a submucosal tumor by ESD was impressive. I had originally planned only to observe examinations, but when I asked "Could I also see ESD and so on?", I could see many interesting treatments, so I felt it was good that I said what I wanted to see.

・Week 3. Outpatient clinic. In observing the outpatient clinic, of course the patients and doctors spoke in Italian, so there were difficult parts, but by chance a kind local student wrote explanations in English on a smartphone for me, and I could deepen my clinical knowledge. Even when that student was not there, when I asked the doctor after the patient had left, they kindly taught me.

・Week 4. Echo. I observed the doctor examining with ultrasound, and the doctor was very kind and taught me many things. After being taught how to read it, in the end I was allowed to apply the ultrasound probe to a patient myself.

In this way, in the four weeks of gastroenterology, although there were elements similar to the internal medicine I did in February, I could learn in a wider range of settings: endoscopy, outpatient clinic and ultrasound. Because I met different settings and doctors every week, every day was fresh and fulfilling.

・Ward. Basically I accompanied them on rounds. I was able to see a wide variety of congenital heart diseases, including very rare ones, in newborns to children, elementary, junior high and high school students, young people and occasionally adults, which became an unforgettable experience. For each patient, the doctor explained the pathology, surgery, medical treatment and so on. After rounds, the doctor sometimes drew diagrams and explained one-on-one.

・HCU. In this somewhat tense setting where immediate postoperative management is carried out, I could watch the doctors examining patients, for example by applying an echo probe, which was a good experience.

・Cath lab. I observed ablation. The doctors, technicians and nurses actively explained, and it was a very fulfilling time. I only learned from a friend near the end of the clerkship that I was allowed into the cath lab too, so I could only go once, but because it was such a fruitful clerkship, I wished I could have visited more often.

・Surgery. I could observe various operations I had never seen before, such as the Glenn procedure for single ventricle and ECMO decannulation. It was a situation unthinkable in Japan, in that I was allowed to observe right next to the surgical field even though I was not sterile, but thanks to that I could always watch surgery up close while hearing explanations directly from the operating doctor, and every time was very enjoyable. The professor was a woman, and she performed many operations and also explained things to me politely, and she was very cool. Also, because it was a joint clerkship of internal medicine and surgery, I was very happy when, on rounds, I could see the baby who had undergone the surgery I had observed doing well on the ward afterward. In this way, in the four weeks of pediatric cardiac surgery I could learn broadly, in the ward, catheter lab, HCU and surgery. Also, I had never had the opportunity to see so many congenital heart disease pathologies and treatments in actual clinical practice before, so I learned a great deal.

First, in terms of the healthcare system, I saw various differences. Here I would like to touch on two points. The first is that Italy has a system of "free medical care." But this is conditional: it means that "once you are diagnosed with a certain disease, the cost of related tests and treatment is free." In other words, regular health checkups cost money. This is very different from the Japanese way of thinking, "have regular tests so that you stay healthy and prevent illness"; I felt that in Italy prevention is not emphasised much and the emphasis is on "treating illness once it occurs." Also, "free" medical care can be received only at public hospitals, but at public hospitals there is a major problem that one has to wait a very long time to receive that care. Because treatment of patients with life-threatening conditions is prioritised, I was told that it is often necessary to wait several months, for example, to undergo surgery for a fracture that is not life-threatening. In the emergency department too, one apparently has to wait a very long time. Therefore, people who want to be treated quickly pay money and go to private hospitals. The second is that every citizen has a family doctor assigned. Citizens can choose their own family doctor. When one feels unwell, one must first consult the family doctor. Then one is referred to a large hospital. Some family doctors apparently disclose their contact information so that they can be reached immediately. Although there are many differences from Japan like this, the Italian friends and host family I spoke to all said they were satisfied with the healthcare system. Next I would like to touch on three differences in the medical setting. The first is that in Italy, within one region, information about patients is shared across the electronic charts of all hospitals. I felt it was groundbreaking that patients can be followed up not only within one hospital but across the whole region. The second is that digitalisation is not yet as advanced as in Japan. Of course they mainly used electronic charts, but I often saw doctors entering the content of paper charts into the electronic chart. Files collecting documents for each patient were also often used. The doctors too said that it is still a period of transition from paper to electronic. The third is that the proportion of women doctors was higher than in Japan. In particular, gastroenterology and cardiac surgery are overwhelmingly male in Japan, but in Italy many women doctors were active in such departments. Seeing this with my own eyes, I wanted to become active like those local women doctors in the future, and at the same time I wanted to think about what is needed to change the environment in Japan, where there are still many departments in which it is hard for women doctors to work.

I made many unforgettable memories in these three months and was able to grow in many respects. I strongly feel that, however difficult a situation I may face in the future, I will surely be able to recall this hard experience and approach it positively. And in these three months I came to love the country of Italy. There were many differences from Japan, but that was very interesting, and I was able to gain new perspectives that I could not have gained if I had not studied in Italy. Also, by studying abroad and interacting with medical students from faraway countries, my world widened and my motivation also grew. I highly recommend studying at the University of Bologna to anyone who wants to be surrounded by kind and cheerful Italians for three months, immerse themselves in a rich culture, and broaden their horizons both in medicine and beyond. Even if you cannot speak Italian, I guarantee that it will definitely be a wonderful study abroad! Of course, I think it would be even more fun if you could speak Italian. I definitely want to visit Italy again in the future, and until then I want to keep studying Italian. Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone in the International Research Office, beginning with Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, who supported this very valuable experience, Dr. イッツェル, who has taught medical English since I entered the university, the doctors, staff and friends of the host University of Bologna, my host family and roommates, and my parents. Thank you very much.
